title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 16
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: An airline reports that 88 per cent of its flights arrived on time last year, up from 79 per cent, and advertises the improvement as evidence of better operations.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the advertisement?
options: A. The airline added several new routes.
B. The airline lengthened its published flight times by twenty minutes, so flights taking the same time as before now count as punctual.
C. Some delays are caused by air traffic control.
D. Competing airlines report similar figures.
E. Punctuality is measured at the gate rather than at take-off.
questions.explanation: Redefining the target converts unchanged performance into an improved statistic; nothing about the operation need have changed.

questions.prompt: A plumbing firm found that apprentices who complete its four-year programme have fewer callbacks on their work than those who complete a two-year programme elsewhere, and argues that longer training produces better plumbers.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the argument?
options: A. How much each programme costs
B. Whether apprentices enjoy the longer programme
C. How many apprentices each programme accepts
D. Whether the two groups work on comparable jobs under comparable supervision
E. Whether the firm employs both groups
questions.explanation: Callback rates depend on the difficulty of the work and the oversight applied; without comparable jobs the comparison measures assignment rather than training.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain replaced plastic lids with a lid-free cup design and reports that its plastic use has fallen by twelve tonnes a year, describing this as a reduction in waste.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the description?
options: A. Spillages rose sharply, and the chain now supplies two paper sleeves and additional napkins with most drinks, whose combined material exceeds the plastic saved.
B. Customers were not consulted about the change.
C. The new cups are slightly more expensive.
D. Some customers bring their own cups.
E. Plastic lids were recyclable in some regions.
questions.explanation: The substitution transfers the material rather than removing it, and the replacement burden is larger. E weakens the environmental case mildly but does not overturn the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A hospital increased the ratio of nurses to patients on its medical wards and reports that patient mortality fell. Administrators conclude that staffing levels affect survival.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. Nurses report lower stress since the change.
B. The hospital also opened a new intensive care unit.
C. The increase was applied to alternating wards in a staggered order, and mortality fell in each ward only after its own staffing rose.
D. Mortality fell nationally over the same period.
E. The additional nurses were newly qualified.
questions.explanation: Ward-by-ward staggering ties the effect to the treatment in both time and place, ruling out the hospital-wide and national explanations that C and D would otherwise supply.

questions.prompt: Every carton of eggs sold under the Wenlow label comes from a farm inspected twice a year. No farm inspected twice a year has been cited for a welfare breach in the past five years. Some farms supplying the Wenlow packing plant have been cited for a welfare breach.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Inspection prevents welfare breaches.
B. Most farms supplying the plant are inspected twice a year.
C. No eggs sold under the Wenlow label come from cited farms in future.
D. Farms inspected once a year are cited more often.
E. Some farms supplying the packing plant do not produce eggs sold under the Wenlow label.
questions.explanation: A cited farm is not inspected twice yearly, and Wenlow-label eggs require such inspection, so the cited farms supply the plant without supplying that label. B asserts causation the statements do not support.

questions.prompt: A city required taxi operators to make a proportion of their fleet wheelchair accessible. Two years later, the total number of licensed taxis had fallen, and wheelchair users report longer waits than before.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this outcome?
options: A. Accessible vehicles are more expensive to purchase and to run, and some operators left the trade rather than meet the requirement.
B. Wheelchair users make more journeys than other passengers.
C. The requirement was announced a year in advance.
D. Some drivers were unfamiliar with the ramps.
E. The city also raised licence fees for private hire vehicles.
questions.explanation: A cost imposed at the fleet level can shrink supply enough to outweigh the composition change, which is exactly the pattern reported.

questions.prompt: A university began recording lectures and found that attendance fell. It concludes that students substitute recordings for attendance and proposes to stop recording.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. Recording equipment is expensive to maintain.
B. Some lecturers dislike being recorded.
C. Recordings are watched most heavily in the week before examinations, and students who watch them attend at the same rate as those who do not.
D. Attendance has fallen at other universities as well.
E. Recordings are available only to enrolled students.
questions.explanation: If viewing concentrates on revision and is unrelated to attendance, removing recordings would remove a revision resource without restoring attendance.

questions.prompt: A wind farm operator reports that bird deaths at its site are lower than at a neighbouring site with the same number of turbines, and attributes the difference to its slower rotor speeds.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the attribution?
options: A. The neighbouring site is older.
B. The neighbouring site lies on a migration route along a ridge, while the operator's site does not.
C. Both sites use turbines from the same manufacturer.
D. Bird deaths are counted by contractors at both sites.
E. Slower rotors generate less electricity.
questions.explanation: Exposure differs enormously between the sites, so the comparison cannot isolate rotor speed. C and D remove other differences rather than adding one.

questions.prompt: A gym found that members who work with personal trainers renew their membership more often, and plans to require every new member to book at least one session with a trainer.
questions.question: The plan assumes which of the following?
options: A. Trainers have capacity for additional sessions.
B. Members enjoy their sessions with trainers.
C. Trainers are paid per session.
D. New members are less fit than existing ones.
E. The renewal difference reflects the effect of training rather than the prior commitment of members who choose to hire a trainer.
questions.explanation: The policy extends a pattern observed among self-selecting members to everyone, which requires that the training, not the disposition, produce the renewal. A is an operational constraint.

questions.prompt: A supermarket introduced refillable containers for detergent and reports that customers who use them buy detergent more frequently than customers who buy bottles. The chain concludes that refills increase detergent consumption.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Refill stations are located near the entrance.
B. Refills are slightly cheaper per litre.
C. Some customers use both refills and bottles.
D. The refill containers hold less than a standard bottle, so a customer using the same quantity of detergent visits the station more often.
E. Detergent sales overall are unchanged.
questions.explanation: Purchase frequency and quantity consumed come apart when the unit size changes; the same usage produces more transactions. E is consistent with this but does not itself explain the frequency difference.

questions.prompt: A museum introduced free audio guides and reports that visitors who take one stay longer than those who do not. The director argues that audio guides make exhibitions more engaging.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of maintaining the guides
B. assumes that a longer visit indicates greater engagement, and that guide users would not have stayed longer anyway
C. does not distinguish between permanent and temporary exhibitions
D. relies on data from a single museum
E. overlooks visitors who bring their own headphones
questions.explanation: The argument makes two leaps at once: duration is treated as engagement, and a self-selected group's behaviour is treated as an effect of the guide.

questions.passageText:
When competing technologies perform the same function and each becomes more valuable as more people adopt it, the market tends not to settle on a stable division. Early leads compound: a format with more users attracts more complementary products, which attracts more users. The outcome is that one standard takes almost everything, and the process is often described as the market selecting the better technology.

That description is too strong. The dynamic favours whatever gets ahead early, and an early lead can come from a licensing decision, a distribution agreement or an accident of timing rather than from technical merit. Cases in which the surviving standard was arguably inferior are among the most cited in the literature, and the more careful of those studies show something narrower than the popular version: not that the market reliably chooses badly, but that it does not reliably choose well, because the mechanism doing the selecting is not primarily comparing.

Firms behave accordingly. They subsidise early adoption, license aggressively to seed complementary products, and sometimes give away the specification, because a standard nobody else builds for is worth little. Each of these sacrifices near-term revenue for position, and the calculation makes sense only under the tipping dynamic.

Two circumstances weaken the pattern. Where users can operate two standards at once, the pressure to converge falls sharply. And where a converter can be built cheaply, the advantage of a large installed base is partly neutralised. Both explain why some markets that appear to invite a single winner have sustained several formats for decades.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the tipping dynamic favours
options: A. the technically superior standard in most cases
B. standards backed by the largest firms
C. open specifications over proprietary ones
D. the standard with the lowest production cost
E. whichever standard gets ahead early, for whatever reason
questions.explanation: The passage says an early lead can come from licensing, distribution or timing rather than merit, and that the selecting mechanism is not primarily comparing.

questions.passageText:
The extinction that removed the non-avian dinosaurs coincides with two events large enough to be candidates: an asteroid impact at Chicxulub, and the eruption of the Deccan Traps, a volcanic province that released enormous quantities of gas over a period surrounding the boundary. The debate over their relative contributions has been unusually productive because each side has had to become quantitative.

The impact case is strong on timing. A worldwide layer enriched in iridium marks the boundary, shocked quartz and glass spherules are distributed consistently with a single event, and the crater has been dated to within the precision available. The mechanism — darkness and cooling from injected material, followed by longer-term effects — is modelled in detail.

The volcanic case is strong on duration. Eruptions of that scale release sulphur and carbon dioxide over tens of thousands of years, producing environmental stress that no single day can match, and there is evidence of ecological disturbance beginning before the boundary in some records.

The most interesting recent work concerns interaction rather than competition. Dating suggests the impact may have coincided with a change in the eruptions' character, and a biosphere already stressed by prolonged volcanism would be more vulnerable to a sudden shock than an undisturbed one. That formulation is harder to test, since it predicts a pattern rather than a single decisive observation, and the field's difficulty now is less a shortage of evidence than the problem of distinguishing hypotheses that make similar predictions about a record with limited resolution.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the impact hypothesis is particularly well supported with respect to
options: A. the duration of environmental stress
B. evidence of disturbance beginning before the boundary
C. the release of sulphur over tens of thousands of years
D. timing, given the boundary layer, shocked quartz and crater dating
E. the resolution of the fossil record
questions.explanation: The passage assigns timing to the impact case and duration to the volcanic one.

questions.passageText:
Requiring a licence to practise an occupation is defended on the ground that customers cannot judge quality in advance and would otherwise be exposed to incompetence. The argument is strongest where the harm from bad work is severe and hard to detect — surgery, aircraft maintenance, electrical installation — and it weakens as those conditions weaken.

Two effects follow from any licence. The intended one is that the least competent practitioners are excluded, so average quality among those practising rises. The unintended one is that the number of practitioners falls and prices rise, which pushes some customers to unlicensed providers or to doing the work themselves. Where the do-it-yourself alternative is more dangerous than an unlicensed practitioner, a licence can raise average quality among professionals while worsening outcomes overall — an effect found in studies of several trades.

The empirical literature also finds that licensing requirements are poorly correlated with the risk the occupation presents. Requirements have expanded into occupations where the case is thin, and the training hours demanded frequently exceed anything the work requires, which is difficult to explain by consumer protection and easy to explain by the interest of incumbents in restricting entry.

The useful policy question is therefore not licensing or nothing. Certification, in which a title is protected but practice is not, preserves the information a licence provides while leaving the choice with the customer, and it is the arrangement that fits most of the occupations where full licensing has been extended.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the case for licensing is strongest where
options: A. the occupation has many practitioners
B. training is inexpensive
C. customers can compare providers easily
D. incumbents support the requirement
E. harm from bad work is severe and hard to detect in advance
questions.explanation: Surgery, aircraft maintenance and electrical installation are given as the examples, and the case weakens as those conditions weaken.

questions.passageText:
A map projects a curved surface onto a flat one, and no projection preserves shape, area, distance and direction at once. This is a mathematical fact rather than a limitation of technique, and it means every map has decided what to distort.

The familiar consequences are well known: the projection long used in classrooms preserves angles, which made it valuable for navigation, and inflates areas away from the equator, which made high-latitude countries appear far larger than they are. Alternatives preserving area distort shape instead, sometimes severely. Neither is correct in the abstract; each is correct for a purpose, and the error is using a map made for one purpose to answer a question it was not built for.

Less familiar is that the choices continue after the projection. What is named and what is left blank, which settlements pass the threshold for inclusion, whether a disputed border is drawn solid, dotted or twice, where the sheet is cut — all are decisions, and all are read by users as description rather than as choice. Maps carry unusual authority precisely because their conventions are invisible to most readers.

None of this makes cartography untrustworthy. It makes a map a compressed argument about what matters, produced under constraints that force selection. The reader who asks what a map was made for, and by whom, is not being cynical; they are reading it in the way its makers, who had to choose, understood perfectly well that it should be read.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that no map can preserve shape, area, distance and direction simultaneously because
options: A. survey data are never complete
B. this is a mathematical consequence of projecting a curved surface onto a flat one
C. printing introduces distortion
D. cartographers disagree about conventions
E. the Earth is not perfectly spherical
questions.explanation: The passage calls it a mathematical fact rather than a limitation of technique.

A map projects a curved surface onto a flat one, and no projection preserves shape, area, distance and direction at once. This is a mathematical fact rather than a limitation of technique, and it means every map has decided what to distort.

The familiar consequences are well known: the projection long used in classrooms preserves angles, which made it valuable for navigation, and inflates areas away from the equator, which made high-latitude countries appear far larger than they are. Alternatives preserving area distort shape instead, sometimes severely. Neither is correct in the abstract; each is correct for a purpose, and the error is using a map made for one purpose to answer a question it was not built for.

Less familiar is that the choices continue after the projection. What is named and what is left blank, which settlements pass the threshold for inclusion, whether a disputed border is drawn solid, dotted or twice, where the sheet is cut — all are decisions, and all are read by users as description rather than as choice. Maps carry unusual authority precisely because their conventions are invisible to most readers.

None of this makes cartography untrustworthy. It makes a map a compressed argument about what matters, produced under constraints that force selection. The reader who asks what a map was made for, and by whom, is not being cynical; they are reading it in the way its makers, who had to choose, understood perfectly well that it should be read.
